messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Aroha

Aroha had been a welder for fifty-three years, since she was a girl of twenty-seven working in the Auckland shipyards. Her hands knew the arc, the metal, the precise angle of a bead. She had raised three children on that wage, and her husband—Hemi, a quieter man who worked in logistics—had always known her as someone capable, someone who could fix things. That was before the last five years with him became something else entirely.

It had started small, as these things do. A shove when she disagreed about money. A closed fist against the kitchen counter one night when dinner was late. Then, three years ago, a night when she had asked him to help her with a leaking tap in the bathroom. He had been drinking. When she repeated herself, he had taken her by the wrist—her dominant wrist, the one that held the torch—and twisted it until she felt something tear deep in the joint. He had held her against the wall by her throat. She remembered the cold tile on her spine and the way her vision narrowed to a single point of light. When he finally released her, she had fallen to the floor, gasping, and he had stepped over her to pour another drink.

She had not reported it. She had not told her children. Instead, she had taped the wrist, waited for the swelling to subside, and returned to work, where she had learned to compensate—favoring her right side, avoiding certain angles, telling her supervisor the pain was arthritis. The injury had never fully healed. Even now, three years later, there was an ache that worsened in the cold, and a weakness she could not quite overcome. That weakness terrified her in a way she could not articulate to anyone. Because Aroha had come to believe that her body was no longer her own, that the damage Hemi had done was permanent and irreversible, that she could no longer trust the signals it sent her or the strength it once possessed. The thought of being trapped again—of her body failing her, of her hands not responding the way they needed to—had begun to colonize her nights.

Sleep had become impossible. She would lie beside Hemi in the dark, her mind cataloging the sounds of the house: the creak of the floorboards, his breathing, the distant hum of the refrigerator. Around 2 a.m., she would wake suddenly, her heart hammering, and she would rise to check the locks on the doors and windows, moving through the rooms in her nightgown like a sentry. Sometimes she would stand in the kitchen for an hour, unable to return to bed. Even within the walls of her own home, she felt exposed, as though the walls themselves had become permeable. The conviction that something terrible would happen again—that she was vulnerable in a way she had never been before—had taken root so deeply that she found herself unable to relax even in daylight. She felt on guard constantly, her shoulders tense, her jaw clenched. This hypervigilance was not paranoia; it was clarity. Her body had been broken once. It could be broken again. The world had shown her that.

The two beliefs fed each other relentlessly. Because she could no longer trust her body, she remained alert, scanning for threat. And because she remained alert—waking in the night, unable to rest, exhausted—she felt more vulnerable, more certain that her body would fail her when it mattered most. At eighty, she had expected to be slowing down naturally, but instead she felt as though she were deteriorating under the weight of constant vigilance. She had also come to believe that the capacity for normal emotion had been burned out of her, that whatever warmth or peace she might have once felt was now ash. She moved through her days with her grandson, with her garden, with a kind of hollow compliance. Nothing brought her joy. Nothing felt safe.

It was her daughter-in-law who finally insisted she speak to someone. Aroha had mentioned, almost in passing, that she was not sleeping well. The concern in that woman's eyes—the way she had leaned forward and asked, gently, if Hemi was still hurting her—had cracked something open. At eighty years old, with hands that had built ships and welded steel, Aroha had finally admitted that she was afraid, and that she no longer knew how to stop being afraid.
